metadata.title: The 512-Token Blind Spot
metadata.audience: Anyone who feeds long text to language models

beats.narration_text: Models read tokens, not words, and can only take in so many. Feed a long document past the limit and the rest is cut off, sometimes mid-thought.

props.command: Why did the model miss the one word that flips the meaning?
output: Long text gets cut to fit a limit.
The qualifier that flips the meaning gets dropped.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Asavari, a fellow at Humanitarians AI. This video is about a subtle bug that causes big mistakes: how a model's token limit can silently drop the one word that flips a sentence's meaning. You'll learn why chunking is a real decision, not a default. If you feed long text to language models, this is for you.

props.command: What is this video about, and why should I watch it?
output: Who: Asavari, a Humanitarians AI fellow
Why watch: catch the mistake before it costs you

beats.narration_text: Picture a sentiment model with a five-hundred-and-twelve-token window reading an earnings statement. The text says revenue grew, and then, just past the cutoff, excluding one-time items. The model scores it as strong growth. It never saw the qualifier. The output is confident, clean, and wrong.

props.artifactTitle: The tokenizer cuts at 512. The qualifier lives at 513
artifactLines: the model reads the first half only
scores it as pure growth — confident, clean, wrong
props.sparkLine: A hard cut in the middle of a meaning.

beats.narration_text: The fix isn't a bigger model, it's treating chunking as a real decision. The naive approach cuts every five hundred and twelve tokens, splitting ideas in half. The better approach splits on meaning, keeping a claim with the qualifier that modifies it, and overlapping chunks so nothing important lands on a boundary.

props.artifactTitle: Chunking is a decision, not a default
props.artifactHeading: chunk on meaning, not on count
artifactLines: Naive: cut every 512 tokens -> splits mid-idea
Meaning-aware: keep a claim with its qualifier; overlap chunks
Where you cut silently determines the answer
props.sparkLine: Where you cut changes the answer.

beats.narration_text: A warning, because people reach for the obvious fix. Newer models have larger windows, but every model still has a limit, and long documents still get truncated. Worse, even within the window, models pay less attention to the middle. A bigger window pushes the boundary out. It doesn't make it disappear.

props.artifactTitle: A bigger window delays the problem
artifactLines: Newer models have larger windows — but every model has a limit
Long inputs still get truncated when they exceed it
Even inside the window, the middle gets less attention

beats.narration_text: Know the token limit and how long your input really is. Look at where your chunks actually cut. Ask whether a qualifier could get separated from its claim. And check the tail of the document. The cutoff is a silent editor of your data. If you don't decide where it falls, it decides for you.

props.artifactTitle: Mind the boundary, or it will mind you
props.artifactHeading: The cutoff is a silent editor of your data
artifactLines: What's the token limit — and how long is your input?
Where do your chunks actually cut?
Could a qualifier be split from its claim?
Did you check the tail, or assume it was read?
